title: 1 Samuel 14:24–35
context: 1 Samuel 14:24–35 turns from the victory to a problem Saul created. Before the battle he had bound the army with an oath: no one was to eat until evening, until he was avenged on his enemies. The exhausted troops obey, even when they find honey in the forest, but Jonathan, who did not hear the oath, eats a little and is refreshed. Told of the oath, he says his father “has troubled the land.” By evening the famished people seize plunder and eat meat with the blood, breaking the law of Leviticus 17 and Deuteronomy 12. Saul acts to correct this, and builds his first altar to the LORD. The narrative presents the oath as rash and harmful, an obstacle to the victory God had given.

verses.text: The men of Israel were distressed that day; for Saul had adjured the people, saying, “Cursed is the man who eats any food until it is evening, and I am avenged of my enemies.” So none of the people tasted food.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul had bound the people: “Cursed is the man who eats any food until it is evening, and I am avenged of my enemies.” Arminian readers note that Saul’s oath places a heavy burden on his men at the very time they need strength. His focus on “my enemies” suggests personal concern rather than God’s glory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the oath binds the army by a curse, invoking God’s name for Saul’s own aims. The narrator comments, “The men of Israel were distressed that day.” Shared ground: both traditions read the oath as rash, in line with Proverbs 20:25, “It is a snare to a man to make a rash dedication,” and both see it hindering the victory.

verses.text: All the people came into the forest; and there was honey on the ground.
verses.arminianNotes: The people come into the forest, “and there was honey on the ground.” Arminian readers note that God’s provision lies within reach of the exhausted soldiers, yet Saul’s oath prevents them from receiving it. The detail sets up the tension of the following verses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that God provides nourishment in abundance while the king’s command forbids it. Human rules can stand in the way of God’s gifts. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as preparing for the conflict between Saul’s oath and the people’s need.

verses.text: When the people had come to the forest, behold, honey was dripping, but no one put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath.
verses.arminianNotes: The honey is dripping, “but no one put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath.” Arminian readers note the people’s scrupulous obedience to the oath despite their hunger. Their fear shows how seriously oaths in God’s name were taken.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the people’s fear of the oath is a form of reverence, even though the oath itself was unwise. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the weight of an oath in Israel and the burden Saul’s command placed on the army.

verses.text: But Jonathan didn’t hear when his father commanded the people with the oath. Therefore he put out the end of the rod that was in his hand and dipped it in the honeycomb, and put his hand to his mouth; and his eyes brightened.
verses.arminianNotes: Jonathan had not heard the oath, so he dips his rod in the honeycomb and eats, “and his eyes brightened.” Arminian readers note that Jonathan acts in ignorance, not defiance. The narrative is careful to establish that he had no knowledge of his father’s command.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the physical refreshment as a sign of what the honey could have done for the whole army. Jonathan’s ignorance means he is not guilty of deliberate disobedience. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as establishing Jonathan’s innocence of intent, which will matter greatly in 14:43–45.

verses.text: Then one of the people answered, and said, “Your father directly commanded the people with an oath, saying, ‘Cursed is the man who eats food today.’ ” So the people were faint.
verses.arminianNotes: A soldier tells Jonathan, “Your father directly commanded the people with an oath,” and the narrator adds, “So the people were faint.” Arminian readers note that Jonathan now learns of the oath after the fact. The people’s faintness shows the cost of Saul’s command.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator places the people’s weakness right beside the report of the oath, linking the two. The oath is undermining the army. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as confirming the harmful effect of the oath and as setting up Jonathan’s response.

verses.text: Then Jonathan said, “My father has troubled the land. Please look how my eyes have brightened because I tasted a little of this honey.
verses.arminianNotes: Jonathan says, “My father has troubled the land,” pointing to how his eyes brightened after a little honey. Arminian readers note that Jonathan speaks frankly about his father’s mistake, judging the oath by its effects on the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that “troubled” is the same verb used of Achan, who “troubled” Israel (compare Joshua 7:25). Jonathan suggests that the real trouble comes from Saul’s rash oath, not from himself. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the narrative’s own evaluation of the oath, voiced through Jonathan.

verses.text: How much more, if perhaps the people had eaten freely today of the plunder of their enemies which they found? For now there has been no great slaughter among the Philistines.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jonathan says, “How much more, if perhaps the people had eaten freely today … For now there has been no great slaughter among the Philistines.” Arminian readers note that Jonathan sees how the oath has limited the victory God had begun. Practical wisdom and faith go together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the oath, meant to secure victory, actually reduces it. Human zeal without wisdom can hinder God’s work. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sound judgment on the oath’s effect, and both see the narrative endorsing Jonathan’s assessment.

verses.text: They struck the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon. The people were very faint;
verses.arminianNotes: Israel strikes the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon, but “The people were very faint.” Arminian readers note that the victory continues, but the exhaustion of the army is now acute. The people’s weakness sets up the sin of the next verse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God gives a wide victory despite the oath, while the people’s weakness shows its cost. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as holding together God’s continuing deliverance and the harm caused by Saul’s command.

verses.text: and the people pounced on the plunder, and took sheep, cattle, and calves, and killed them on the ground; and the people ate them with the blood.
verses.arminianNotes: The people pounce on the plunder, kill animals on the ground, and eat them “with the blood.” Arminian readers note that extreme hunger drives the people to break God’s law. Saul’s rash oath has led to real sin among the people, even though each person remained responsible for what he ate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the law: “You shall not eat the blood of any kind of flesh; for the life of all flesh is its blood” (Leviticus 17:14). The people’s sin is real, yet it grows out of the king’s rash oath. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing how one unwise command can lead others into sin.

verses.text: Then they told Saul, saying, “Behold, the people are sinning against the LORD, in that they eat meat with the blood.” He said, “You have dealt treacherously. Roll a large stone to me today!”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul is told, “the people are sinning against the LORD, in that they eat meat with the blood.” He says, “You have dealt treacherously. Roll a large stone to me today!” Arminian readers note that Saul responds to the people’s sin with concern, though he does not acknowledge his own part in causing it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note Saul’s zeal to correct the people’s sin, which is right in itself, while the narrative leaves the reader aware that his oath created the crisis. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing a king concerned for ritual purity but unaware of his own responsibility.

verses.text: Saul said, “Disperse yourselves among the people, and tell them, ‘Every man bring me here his ox, and every man his sheep, and kill them here, and eat; and don’t sin against the LORD in eating meat with the blood.’ ” All the people brought every man his ox with him that night, and killed them there.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul orders each man to bring his ox and sheep to be slaughtered properly, “and don’t sin against the LORD in eating meat with the blood.” Arminian readers note that Saul’s measure allows the people to eat lawfully. The people respond and bring their animals that night.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the large stone provides a proper place of slaughter so the blood can be drained, in keeping with Deuteronomy 12:16: “you shall not eat the blood. You shall pour it out on the earth like water.” Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sensible remedy for the people’s sin.

verses.text: Saul built an altar to the LORD. This was the first altar that he built to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Saul built an altar to the LORD. This was the first altar that he built to the LORD.” Arminian readers note that Saul turns to worship, an outward sign of devotion. The narrator’s note that this was his first altar may hint at how late it came in his reign, though the text does not say why he had not built one before.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator records the altar without praise or blame. Saul’s religious acts are real, but the narrative repeatedly shows them disconnected from patient obedience. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing Saul’s religious concern, while noting that the narrative keeps the reader alert to the gap between ritual and obedience.
